source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Explain the generic memory-management distinction between heap and stack without silently narrowing the answer to one language/runtime. Compare lifetime, allocation/reclamation, organization, concurrency, failure modes and performance, and explicitly separate common implementation patterns from universal guarantees.

sources.title: Linux man-pages alloca(3)
anchors: alloca allocates size bytes in the stack frame of the caller
space allocated by alloca is automatically freed when the calling function returns
stack overflow behavior is possible when the stack frame cannot be extended

sources.title: Linux man-pages malloc(3)
anchors: malloc dynamically allocates memory and free releases a previously allocated block
allocation can fail when memory cannot be allocated
dynamic allocation has a lifetime independent of a single caller stack frame until released

sources.title: Java Virtual Machine Specification 26 §2.5.2 Java Virtual Machine Stacks
anchors: each JVM thread has a private JVM stack created with the thread
JVM stacks store frames and are involved in method invocation and return
excessive stack-depth demand can cause StackOverflowError

sources.title: Java Virtual Machine Specification 26 §2.5.3 Heap
anchors: the JVM heap is shared among JVM threads
class instances and arrays are allocated from the JVM heap at the specification level
heap storage is reclaimed by automatic storage management and the specification does not mandate a particular GC algorithm or contiguous layout

claims.text: The generic distinction is primarily a lifetime and management-model distinction: stack storage commonly follows structured call-frame lifetime, while dynamic/heap storage supports allocations whose lifetime need not end with the allocating call.

Stack-frame storage can commonly be reclaimed as the call frame exits, whereas dynamic allocations require an independent release policy such as explicit free, ownership/region management or managed-runtime garbage collection.

Concrete runtimes may define the abstractions differently. The JVMS, for example, specifies a private JVM stack per thread and a shared managed heap for class instances and arrays; these JVM-specific guarantees must not be promoted to universal rules for every language/runtime.
Stack exhaustion and dynamic-allocation exhaustion are distinct failure classes, while their exact manifestation is language/runtime specific.

writer_constraints: Answer the frozen generic heap-vs-stack wording first; do not silently turn it into a JVM-only or C-only question.
Organize the distinction by lifetime, allocation/reclamation, organization, concurrency, failure modes and performance mechanisms.
Use wording such as usually/commonly when describing implementation patterns that are not language-independent guarantees.

Do not claim that every local variable is physically on a stack or every source-language object is physically allocated on a heap; compiler/runtime optimization can change physical placement or eliminate allocations.
Do not claim that every heap object is automatically shared by all threads; object sharing depends on reference publication and runtime semantics.
Do not claim stack allocation is universally faster; explain the common pointer/frame-management advantage while preserving implementation/workload dependence.
Do not attach fixed stack or heap sizes to the generic answer.
Do not fabricate production incidents, allocator settings, GC metrics or project experience.
